_about: Who a situation involves. nouns are captured (so 'my sister' becomes 'your sister' in the reply); cues only detect. Patterns use the small matching language described in tools/chat/README.md: | separates choices, * ends a word stem, .. allows a few words in between, <a|b> captures. Text may use {them}, {Them}, {they}, {their}.

self.fit: Everything in the program starts with you. You can do all of this on your own: check your own weather, learn your wiring, and plan what settles you. Here’s a gentle path for just you.
path: Today’s Weather: a one-minute check on yourself
self.step: Check your battery before you judge yourself: is this about the thing, or about everything else you’re carrying today?

partner.cues: we re married|we are married|my marriage|our marriage|our relationship
partner.fit: With a partner, the unseen work is often the heaviest part. Start by seeing who does what, then give each regular job one owner, then keep small things small with a short daily check-in.
path: Who did what (WP-01, a week’s log)
partner.step: Pick a calm time you both agree on, not the middle of a busy evening, and keep it to one topic.

steps.distance: Try one small ritual that’s just yours: ten minutes after dinner, phones down, to catch up on each other’s day.
steps.load: Suggest you each log one ordinary week in Who did what (WP-01), separately, and only then compare.

family.cues: my family|our family|family dinner|family group chat|at the holidays|at christmas|at thanksgiving
family.fit: Families often clash on tone and urgency more than on the task itself. Agree who owns what, so nobody has to guess, and test tricky messages before you send them.
family.step: Remember that old family roles show up fast. It’s okay to respond as the adult you are now, not the role you had growing up.

kid.fit: With kids and teens, keep it warm, short and practical. Give them real, age-sized jobs they own, notice their bids for attention, and never ask a child to keep track of what the adults do.
path: Turning Toward: seven small ways to connect
One owner per job (WP-03, age-sized jobs)
kid.step: Talk side by side, not face to face: in the car, on a walk, while cooking. It lowers the pressure for a lot of kids and teens.

steps.distance: Be around without an agenda: hang out where they are, and let them bring things up.
steps.mess: Agree on a small, clear standard for their space and one shared job they fully own.

coparent.fit: A court order or parenting plan always comes first. Inside it, keep handoffs short and calm, keep messages about logistics, give each task one owner, and never use the kids as messengers.
path: One owner per job (WP-03, who handles what)
coparent.step: Keep messages brief, factual and about the kids’ logistics. Save anything bigger for a planned conversation, never at the handoff and never through the kids.

roommate.cues: house share|shared house|shared apartment|shared flat|house meeting
roommate.fit: Roommates do best with a shared picture and clear owners. List the week’s jobs on the Lemonade Stand (it works for two to eight people), give each job one owner, and hold a short house meeting now and then.
roommate.step: Make it about the house, not the person: “our kitchen”, “our bills”, with a short list everyone can see.

steps.money: Put shared costs on the Lemonade Stand’s money side, so everyone sees the same numbers.
steps.group: With three or more of you, hold a 20-minute house meeting with one short list, and give every job one owner before you leave the room.

coworker.cues: at work|in meetings|in the meeting|meetings|standup|stand up|slack|microsoft teams|the office|work chat|my job|at my job|workplace|team of [0-9]+|team of (three|four|five|six|seven|eight)
coworker.fit: At work, the same ideas fit with lighter words. Give every recurring task one clear owner, test tricky messages before you send them, and keep repair quick and professional. The Lemonade Stand and one-owner-per-job both work for teams of two to eight.
coworker.step: Keep it about the work and the process, and put what you agree in a short written note afterward so nobody has to remember it the same way.

steps.group: For a team, run a short retro: what went well, what slipped, and one owner for each fix. One owner per job (WP-03) scales to a team of seven easily.

friend.fit: Friendships run on small, freely given moments. Notice when they reach for you, say what you mean kindly, and check texts before a tone misunderstanding grows.
friend.step: Friendships have no rulebook, so say what you’d like plainly and kindly. Most friends are glad to know.

caregiving.fit: Caregiving is real work, and it’s easy to stop noticing your own battery. Check your own state first, give care tasks named owners (other family, friends, services), and plan what settles you before the hard days.
path: One owner per job (WP-03, share the care tasks)
caregiving.step: Ask for one specific kind of help, with a time: “Could you take Thursday’s appointment?” lands much better than “I need more help.”

other.fit: Whoever it is, the same order helps: see the whole load, fix the setup rather than the person, check your state, and say it so it lands.
other.step: Start from “we’re on the same side, against the problem”, and keep it to one topic at a time.
